en.title: Inviting someone
en.summary: How to ask someone to join you.

paragraphs: We invite people to dinner, to a party or to go out. Sara invites her colleague Mark.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.text: Mark, are you free on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.text: Would you like to come to dinner at my place? I'm cooking at seven.

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: That sounds great. Can I bring something?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.text: Just yourself. Or a dessert, if you like.

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: I'll bring a dessert. Thank you for inviting me.

paragraphs: **1. Would you like to... invites politely.** Use would you like to and the base form: Would you like to come? A friend can also say Do you want to come? or Why don't you come? See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

blocks.html:
StyleInvitation
politeWould you like to come to dinner?
friendlyDo you want to come?
suggestionWhy don't we meet on Saturday?

paragraphs: **2. The future gives the time of the plan.** For a fixed plan use the present continuous: I'm cooking at seven. For a promise or an offer, use will: I'll bring a dessert. See Introduction to Grammar: Future.

items: Say **at my place** or **at my house** for an invitation to your home.
**Are you free on Saturday?** checks that a person has no other plans.
**Can I bring something?** is a polite way to offer to help.

paragraphs: In many English-speaking countries it is common to invite guests a few days before. A guest who says "Just come" may expect you to bring a small gift.
